title: How to automate AP accruals: steps, rules, and software
summary: Learn how to automate AP accruals, from capturing goods received not invoiced to calculating, approving, posting, and reversing entries.
body_markdown:
Key takeaways


- AP accruals account for goods or services received before the related invoice is recorded.
- Automation identifies uninvoiced receipts and prepares accrual entries using defined accounting rules.
- AP shifts from building the schedule manually to reviewing exceptions and supporting documentation.
- Zip's[controller's guide to the continuous close](https://zip.com/resources/continuous-close-guide) explains how connected procure-to-pay data can reduce month-end work.


Accrual automation helps accounts payable (AP) teams find incurred expenses that have not yet been recorded and prepare supported entries for review. Automated accruals use purchase orders (POs) and receipt records to recognize those expenses in the correct period.


When that information is spread across reports and spreadsheets, AP has to reconstruct the company’s outstanding obligations every month. AP accrual automation connects purchasing and receipt data continuously, applies calculation rules, and prepares entries for review. A more complete accrual package reaches accounting sooner as a result.


## **What is accrual automation?**


**Accrual automation uses software to collect evidence of incurred expenses and calculate proposed entries under company policy.** It connects purchasing records with accounting review, so teams can prepare supported accruals throughout the period.


Accrual *accounting* is the method of recognizing revenue and expenses when they are earned or incurred. Accrual automation is the tooling used to prepare and manage the entries that apply that method.


## **What does AP own in the accrual process?**


**AP usually owns the transaction-level information needed to identify expenses that belong in the current accounting period.** The exact responsibilities vary by company, but AP often prepares the accrual schedule that accounting reviews and posts.


Depending on the available data, AP may handle goods received not invoiced (GRNI), contract-based accruals, travel and expense (T&E) accruals, and corporate card accruals.


For PO-backed purchases, AP compares open POs with goods receipts or service confirmations. A received item that has not been invoiced may require an accrual, depending on the company’s materiality policy and accounting rules.


AP may also reconcile vendor statements to find outstanding balances that were not invoiced before the cutoff. Corporate card and T&E activity can enter the same review when charges have been incurred but have not reached the general ledger.


The final output is a supported accrual schedule. It shows the vendor, PO, amount, accounting period, and basis for each estimate. That ownership makes accrual management an AP concern as well as an accounting one.


## **Where does the manual AP accrual process break?**


Manual accrual processes depend on AP finding and interpreting incomplete transactions under a tight deadline. Four problems come up most often.


- Open PO aging requires manual analysis. An[open PO report](https://zip.com/blog/purchase-order-tracking) does not show what was delivered during the period. AP has to compare PO dates with receipt records and decide which balances still represent valid commitments.
- Three-way matching starts too late. Three-way matching compares the PO, receipt, and invoice after an invoice arrives. If goods or services were received without an invoice, there is nothing to match, so AP has to estimate the obligation from purchasing and receipt data.
- Missing information turns into a follow-up campaign. AP emails vendors to ask whether work was completed and requesters to ask whether items arrived. Some answers come in after accounting needs to close the period, and some never come in at all.
- Reversals require separate tracking. When an invoice posts in the following period, someone has to find the related accrual and reverse it. A missed or incorrect reversal can leave expenses or liabilities overstated.


## **Common types of accruals AP teams handle**


The calculation depends on the evidence available and the expense incurred by the cutoff. Coverage varies by platform, so confirm which of these types a tool supports before you rely on it.


Type Trigger Data source How the accrual is calculated


GRNI Goods received before the invoice is recorded PO lines and goods receipts Received quantity × PO unit price, less amounts already recorded


Contract and service Services delivered but not yet invoiced Contract and service confirmations Delivered time or approved milestones × contract rate, less amounts recorded


T&E and card Costs incurred but not yet recorded Expense reports and card feeds Supported charges incurred by the cutoff, excluding amounts already posted


Recurring costs Utilities or professional fees incurred before billing Service terms and prior bills Usage or time-based estimate under company policy, adjusted for current evidence


‍


Payroll accruals usually sit outside AP and rely on payroll records.


## **Accrued vs. prepaid expenses**


An accrued expense records a cost already incurred before payment or invoicing. A prepaid expense starts as an asset because the company paid before receiving the full benefit. It then becomes an expense as that benefit is consumed.


## **How does AP accrual automation work?**


Accounts payable accrual automation connects activity across the purchasing process, so AP does not have to rebuild the same picture at every close. Most systems follow five steps.


### **1. Capture receipts continuously**


When a goods receipt or service confirmation is recorded, the system associates it with the matching PO line. If the invoice has not arrived, the line is marked as received but not invoiced.


AP gets a running view of potential accruals instead of pulling a new report at month-end.


### **2. Apply accrual rules**


The system calculates a proposed accrual according to company policy. A fully received PO line may be accrued at its remaining uninvoiced value. A partial receipt may generate a proportional accrual.


Here is an example. A $30,000 engagement runs 90 days, and services are delivered evenly. The engagement begins in the final month of the closing period, and 10 days of service have been delivered by the cutoff. Nothing has been invoiced or recorded. The proposed accrual is $30,000 ÷ 90 × 10 = $3,333.33.


After approval, the period-end journal entry is a debit to professional services expense of $3,333.33 and a credit to accrued liabilities of $3,333.33. If company policy calls for a day-one reversal, the next period’s entry is a debit to accrued liabilities of $3,333.33 and a credit to professional services expense of $3,333.33.


If the invoice is still missing at the next close, the obligation is reassessed, and the remaining unrecorded amount is accrued. When services are not delivered evenly, milestone or completion evidence is the better basis for the estimate.


### **3. Assemble the accrual package**


At the close date, the system prepares a draft schedule for AP. Each proposed entry can include the supplier, PO number, amount, accounting period, and supporting receipt information. AP reviews exceptions and estimates instead of building the schedule line by line.


Lines without adequate support still need an answer from someone. In Zip,[an agent asks the PO owner or vendor directly](https://zip.com/blog/zip-accrual-automations) and uses the response to build the estimate, so AP is not the one sending reminder emails.


### **4. Approve and post entries**


Once AP or the controller approves the schedule, entries move to the enterprise resource planning (ERP) system through an integration or an approved export.


Approval records and supporting documents should stay attached to the transaction. That creates a traceable record for internal reviews and Sarbanes-Oxley Act (SOX) controls.


### **5. Reverse the accrual**


When the supplier invoice arrives and matches the underlying PO and receipt, the related accrual is identified for reversal. Accounting records the actual invoice expense without leaving the estimate on the books.


When the invoice differs from the estimate, accounting compares the actual charge with the accrued amount and investigates the variance. In the example above, suppose a $3,500 invoice arrives for the same service period. Reversing the $3,333.33 estimate and recording the $3,500 invoice captures the $166.67 difference. Finance then decides whether the variance is a change in estimate or an error that needs correction under its accounting policy.


## **What to look for in accrual automation software**


When you evaluate accrual automation software, ask vendors to show how their software calculates, approves, posts, and reverses accruals. Test each of these with a representative transaction from your own books.


- Source data. The software connects POs, receipts, and contracts, and it flags missing inputs or changes before calculating an accrual.
- Calculation rules. Calculation methods and materiality thresholds can be set by expense type, with controls for canceled or unfulfilled purchases.
- Supporting records. Each proposed entry carries its source records and calculation rationale, so a reviewer can reproduce the amount.
- Approvals. Entries route to the right accounting owner, and approval is recorded before posting.
- ERP posting. The legal entity, general ledger account, and cost center carry into the ERP. Rejected entries are handled in a defined way.
- Reversals. The vendor can show whether reversals are scheduled automatically or require a separate action, and how the software keeps an accrual and its invoice from recording the same expense twice.
- Audit history. Source data, rule changes, and approvals are retained for SOX controls and audit review.

## **What does automation give AP teams back?**


**The immediate benefit is time.** The system assembles the initial schedule, so AP spends close week validating unusual transactions and incomplete records.


Automation also improves completeness by checking receipt and invoice status across the full PO population. Items are less likely to disappear because someone overlooked a row in an aging report.


AP also gets visibility before close. A continuously updated view of received but uninvoiced activity helps the team estimate the accrual liability during the month. ## **Frequently asked questions**


### What is the difference between an AP accrual and a standard journal entry?


An AP accrual records an expense and the related liability before the supplier invoice is posted. A journal entry is the accounting mechanism used to record that accrual or any other adjustment in the general ledger.


### How do AP accruals work with three-way matching?


Three-way matching validates an invoice against a PO and receipt. AP accruals cover the earlier period, after goods or services arrive and before the invoice does. Once the invoice arrives, matching confirms the actual amount and starts the accrual reversal.


### At what dollar threshold should AP automate accruals?


There is no universal threshold. The right amount depends on the company’s materiality policy, transaction volume, and close controls. Automation is most useful when AP has to evaluate a large population of open POs, even if only some items exceed the posting threshold.[PO-backed spend](https://zip.com/blog/purchase-order-management) is usually the best place to start because it has the cleanest source data.


### How does AP accrual automation handle partial receipts?


The system calculates the accrual from the quantity or value received rather than the full PO amount. For service-based purchases, it may apply a percentage or time-based rule that reflects work completed during the period.
